fast-website.title: How to build a fast website
fast-website.summary: Speed is not a feature you add at the end; it is the result of three decisions made on day one.
fast-website.body: ## Why speed matters A visitor who waits three seconds usually does not come back. Speed is not a feature bolted on at the end of a project; it is the result of decisions taken from the very first day. ## The three decisions that matter most - **Size your images correctly.** A 4 MB image displayed in a 400-pixel frame does not just waste bandwidth — it makes the page feel broken. - **Keep the font light.** One variable family with a limited weight range beats four separate files. - **Defer your JavaScript.** Work that is not needed for the first paint must not hold up the first paint. ## Measure, do not guess Before optimising anything, get a number. If you do not know how long the page currently takes, you cannot say whether the change you made was better or worse. ```html ``` > What is not measured does not improve. ## In summary Speed is decided in the structure of a project from the start. The three decisions above make the largest difference with no extra tooling at all.

wordpress-vs-code.title: WordPress or hand-coded: which is right for your project?
wordpress-vs-code.summary: WordPress ships a working site in days and hand-coding buys full control. The real difference is not launch speed; it is the five-year cost and the wall you eventually hit.
wordpress-vs-code.body:
## The wrong question, and the right one

The argument is always the same: WordPress or code? But that question has no good
answer, because both are tools and a tool without a goal means nothing. The right
question is this: over the next two years, what hurts your business more — starting
late, or getting stuck inside a structure you cannot change?

Those two answers are usually not the same one, which is why the argument runs so
long.

## What WordPress actually does

WordPress is a content management system: a database, an admin panel, a theme
system and several thousand ready-made plugins. For a site whose content changes
often and whose shape is settled, that combination is genuinely efficient. An
editor with no technical background can publish an article, swap a photo and build
a menu. Handing the project over is easy too, because anyone who knows WordPress
can pick it up.

The hidden cost shows up when the site leaves the generic template: every plugin is
a dependency, every dependency is a failure point, and every update can break the
site.

## What hand-coding actually does

With a custom build you build only what you need. A page that takes a heavy theme
and four plugins in WordPress can be one HTML file and a little CSS that opens in
under a second.

The price is that every later change needs a developer. If nobody on your team can
write an article, a custom site with no admin panel can quietly become an abandoned
site — that is a failure too, just a slower one.

## Side by side

| Measure | WordPress | Hand-coded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time to first publish | days to weeks | weeks to months |
| Cost to start | low | higher |
| Page speed | average; depends on theme and plugins | entirely in your control |
| Editing content without a developer | yes, through the admin panel | only if a panel is built |
| Custom forms or logic | a plugin, or code inside the theme | part of the original design |
| Security | a wide attack surface; constant updates needed | smaller, more specific surface |
| Five-year running cost | plugins, licences, updates | hosting and code maintenance |
| Dependence on people | low; a large market | high; a specific team or contractor |

Nothing in that table wins. Every row is a cost, and your project can afford some
of these costs and not others.

## Where the decision actually lands

Answer three questions honestly:

1. **How often does the content change?** If it changes several times a week, the
   WordPress admin panel is a real saving.
2. **Does the site's logic go beyond what templates cover?** If it does, every day
   you stay on WordPress raises the cost of pulling away.
3. **Who maintains this site next year?** If the answer is "nobody", the simplest
   structure available is the best choice, not the most advanced one.

## The third option nobody mentions

This is not a binary. A custom build with a light admin panel for the parts that
really do change gives you the speed and control of code and frees the editor from
the developer at the same time. It costs something between the two extremes, and
for most real projects the balance point sits right there.

## In short

WordPress suits a site whose content is heavy and whose shape is fixed. Hand-coded
suits a site whose shape and behaviour are part of its value. If you are not sure
which you are, start with the smallest version that works: the right decision can
be made later, but a structure chosen badly can only be replaced at a price.
